title: Claude Opus 5.5 Composes 25-Minute Symphony in 2,400 Rounds
summary: Dan Price used Claude Opus 5.5 to compose a four-movement orchestral symphony, consuming 35B tokens across 2,400 critic rounds. The actor-critic method used
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- Dan Price used Claude Opus 5.5 to compose a 25-minute, four-movement orchestral symphony consuming approximately 35 billion Opus tokens over one month.
- The system paired one composer agent with multiple critic agents across 2,400 iteration rounds, each referencing orchestration textbooks and master scores.
- The entire score was authored in LilyPond text notation so Claude could edit it programmatically, treating music composition as a code-editing task.


Dan Price has pushed[Claude Opus 5.5](https://emergent.sh/learn/claude-opus-5-5-benchmarks) to its creative limits, producing a fully orchestrated four-movement symphony that consumed approximately 35 billion Opus tokens over the course of a month. The 25-minute composition, complete with 929 bars and 22,979 notes, was refined through roughly 2,400 rounds of iteration using an[actor-critic](https://emergent.sh/glossary/actor-critic) architecture that paired one composer agent with multiple specialized critics. Officially launched on November 25, 2026, the project demonstrates how iteration volume can substitute for verification when evaluating unverifiable creative outputs like music and art.


## Actor-Critic Architecture at Scale


The composition system employed a novel multi-agent approach where one Claude instance acted as the composer while separate Claude instances served as critics, each specializing in a single domain: melody, harmony, orchestration, or playability. Each critic was assigned specific chapters from standard orchestration and harmony textbooks, requiring them to cite rules when proposing changes. For example, one orchestration textbook specifies that two horns are needed to balance one trumpet in loud passages. A critic checked every loud brass chord against this rule, identified three chords with weak important notes, and proposed fixes that the composer accepted.


The critics also compared each movement against master works by Beethoven, Dvořák, and Tchaikovsky every tenth round, answering one question: would a conductor believe a master wrote this? The iterative refinement process initially targeted 50 rounds but continued when improvements remained evident, eventually reaching approximately 600 rounds per movement across four movements. A written log recorded every decision to prevent later critics from undoing earlier refinements.


## LilyPond Text Notation as Code


The entire score was written in LilyPond, a free program that converts typed text into printed sheet music. This text-based approach allowed Claude to edit musical notation the same way programmers edit code. A note is represented as a letter and number (c4 for a C quarter note), enabling Claude to compare versions, run small verification programs, and iterate on the composition programmatically. Because Claude cannot click notes onto a staff or hear audio, treating the score as editable text solved a fundamental interface problem.


The same LilyPond source file produces both the printed score and a basic computer playback, allowing Price to listen to iterations even though Claude itself cannot process audio. Claude judged the music purely from the written score and textbook rules, while Price provided a small number of change requests based on listening to computer-generated playbacks.


## Mockup Production and Audio Refinement


After composing the score, Claude produced four high-quality mockups using REAPER (a digital audio workstation) and EastWest Hollywood Orchestra (a library of pre-recorded orchestral samples). Claude wrote scripts that read the LilyPond score and automatically built each REAPER project, placing every note and mixing all tracks. Because Claude cannot listen to audio, it measured properties that can be quantified: peak loudness, dynamic range, spectral balance, and silence gaps.


The mockup refinement process ran for 184 rounds across four movements, with each round following four steps: render audio, measure properties, identify issues against rules, and adjust the REAPER project. Price supplemented the measurements by listening and providing feedback on issues the metrics missed, such as timpani rolls drowning out other instruments, overly harsh accents, and recordings that sounded too quiet on AirPods. Each human note became a new measurable rule for the critics.


## Release Date and Availability


The complete symphony, mockup recordings, source scores, critic reviews, and production scripts were officially released on November 25, 2026, via GitHub and YouTube. The project used Claude Code Projects (beta), which Price found particularly useful for the orchestrator/thread model, with each movement owned by a dedicated thread. The virtual instrument rendering is available on YouTube, where viewers can select 1080p or higher resolution for sharper score visibility.


## What This Means


Price's experiment demonstrates that iteration volume can serve as a proxy for verification on tasks where objective correctness cannot be measured. The 2,400-round refinement process yielded a composition where only about 14% to 61% of notes from the initial version survived to the final score, depending on the movement. The actor-critic loop, grounded in textbook rules and master score comparisons, enabled Claude Opus 5.5 to produce a symphonic work that Price believes could pass for the work of a human master composer. The project suggests that for creative AI applications, the man who refines a single output 2,500 times may achieve superior results to the man who generates 2,500 single-shot outputs.
